questions.stem: In psychological development, hereditary factors are best described as:
options: the family customs and values handed down from one generation
characteristics passed on from biological parents through genes
the experiences and conditions a person is exposed to after birth
behaviours a child learns by watching and copying their parents
questions.explanation: Hereditary factors are genetic: they are inherited from biological parents through genes. Behaviours learnt by watching parents and family customs are passed on through experience, so they are environmental factors even though they come from the family.

questions.stem: Identical twins Sam and Jo were separated at birth. Sam was raised in a home with many books and conversations; Jo was raised in a neglectful home. As adults, Sam scores much higher on cognitive tests. This best illustrates that:
options: environment can influence how a genetic potential is expressed
heredity alone determines a person's cognitive abilities as an adult
identical twins never share psychological characteristics
cognitive development is fixed at birth and cannot change
questions.explanation: Identical twins have the same genes, so a large difference between them points to the influence of their different environments on how that shared genetic potential developed. It does not show that heredity alone decides ability, because the genes were the same and the outcomes differed.

questions.stem: Ruby inherited a tendency towards a quick temper. Her parents stay calm, model coping strategies and praise her when she manages her frustration. By adolescence she regulates her emotions well. Which statement best describes Ruby's development?
options: Her environment replaced the influence of her genes entirely
Her temperament was learnt, so it was never hereditary at all
Her calm parents passed calmness on to her through their genes
Hereditary and environmental factors interacted to shape it
questions.explanation: Ruby's inherited temperament was the starting point, and her environment influenced how it was expressed, so the two interacted. Saying her environment replaced her genes entirely ignores that the tendency was still there to be managed; development comes from the interaction, not from one factor cancelling the other.

questions.stem: According to the biopsychosocial approach, psychological development and mental wellbeing are best understood as:
options: the product of social factors once a child begins attending school
set by psychological factors, as biology and society only add stress
the result of interacting biological, psychological and social factors
mainly determined by genes, with social factors playing only a minor role
questions.explanation: The biopsychosocial approach is a holistic model: biological, psychological and social factors interact and influence one another. Models that put one type of factor first, such as genes, are the single-cause views that the biopsychosocial approach was developed to replace.

questions.stem: Mei becomes anxious before exams because she tends to think, 'If I fail this, my whole future is ruined.' In the biopsychosocial approach, this way of thinking is a:
options: biological factor
social factor
environmental factor
psychological factor
questions.explanation: Thoughts, beliefs and thinking patterns such as catastrophising are psychological factors. A biological factor would be something physical, such as genes or hormone levels, and a social factor would involve other people or the wider environment.

questions.stem: A researcher explains a young man's depression by listing his family history of depression, his low self-esteem and his recent loss of a job. Why is this a biopsychosocial explanation rather than a biological one?
options: It shows that his low self-esteem was inherited from his family members
It combines a genetic factor with a cognitive factor and an environmental factor
It shows that the depression was caused by genes and triggered by the job loss
It uses only factors that can be measured with a brain scan or blood test
questions.explanation: Family history is a biological factor, low self-esteem is a psychological factor and job loss is a social factor, so the explanation draws on all three. A purely biological explanation would rely on genes or brain chemistry alone, and saying the depression was simply caused by genes leaves out how the factors interact.

questions.stem: In emotional development, attachment refers to:
options: the emotional bond formed between an infant and their main caregiver
an infant's ability to manage strong emotions without help from any adult
a child's understanding that hidden objects continue to exist
the stage when an adolescent forms a clear sense of identity
questions.explanation: Attachment is the close emotional bond between an infant and a caregiver, which gives the infant a secure base. Understanding that hidden objects still exist is object permanence, a part of cognitive development rather than emotional development.

questions.stem: In Harlow's experiments, infant rhesus monkeys spent most of their time clinging to a cloth-covered surrogate mother, even when only a wire surrogate provided milk. This suggested that attachment depends mainly on:
options: the first object seen after birth
the caregiver's size and shape
the comfort of physical contact
being fed by the caregiver
questions.explanation: The monkeys went to the wire surrogate only to feed and spent the rest of their time on the cloth surrogate, which showed that contact comfort mattered more than food. The idea that attachment comes from being fed was the view Harlow's findings challenged.

questions.stem: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, a one-year-old is upset when his mother leaves the room, seeks her out as soon as she returns, and is quickly comforted. Which attachment type does he show?
options: insecure-avoidant
insecure-resistant
disorganised
secure
questions.explanation: Secure attachment is shown by distress at separation followed by seeking comfort and being soothed quickly on reunion. An insecure-resistant infant is also very distressed at separation, but is hard to settle on reunion and may resist being comforted.

questions.stem: In the Strange Situation, a toddler becomes extremely distressed when his father leaves. When the father returns, the toddler clings to him but also pushes him away angrily and cannot be settled. Which attachment type does this best match?
options: insecure-resistant
insecure-avoidant
disorganised
secure
questions.explanation: Strong distress followed by a mixture of seeking and resisting contact, and difficulty being soothed, is the insecure-resistant (or ambivalent) pattern. It differs from disorganised attachment, where behaviour lacks any consistent pattern and the infant may appear dazed or fearful of the caregiver.

questions.stem: Which list gives Piaget's stages of cognitive development in the correct order?
options: pre-operational, sensorimotor, concrete operational, formal operational
sensorimotor, concrete operational, pre-operational, formal operational
pre-operational, sensorimotor, formal operational, concrete operational
sensorimotor, pre-operational, concrete operational, formal operational
questions.explanation: Piaget's stages run from sensorimotor in infancy, to pre-operational in early childhood, to concrete operational in middle childhood, to formal operational from about adolescence. The pre-operational stage comes after the sensorimotor stage because it begins once symbolic thought, such as language, has developed.

questions.stem: A four-month-old reaches for a toy, but as soon as a blanket is placed over it she stops looking and turns away. Which ability has she not yet developed?
options: object permanence
conservation
reversibility
abstract reasoning
questions.explanation: Object permanence is the understanding that objects still exist when they cannot be seen, and it develops during the sensorimotor stage. Conservation and reversibility are later achievements of the concrete operational stage, so they are not what this young infant's behaviour is testing.

questions.stem: Jack, aged five, watches juice being poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass. He then says the tall glass has more juice. This error shows that Jack lacks:
options: conservation
object permanence
symbolic thought
goal-directed behaviour
questions.explanation: Conservation is the understanding that an amount stays the same when its appearance changes, and children usually master it in the concrete operational stage. Jack already has object permanence and symbolic thought, which develop earlier, so they do not explain this particular error.

questions.stem: In Piaget's three-mountains task, four-year-old Ava is asked what a doll on the opposite side of a model can see. She describes her own view. This illustrates:
options: animism
conservation
object permanence
egocentrism
questions.explanation: Egocentrism in Piaget's sense is the inability to see a situation from another person's point of view, which is typical of the pre-operational stage. Animism is a different pre-operational feature: giving lifelike qualities to non-living objects.

questions.stem: Lucas can conserve number and volume and can mentally reverse operations, but he struggles with problems about abstract, hypothetical situations. In which of Piaget's stages is he?
options: pre-operational
formal operational
sensorimotor
concrete operational
questions.explanation: Conservation and reversibility are achieved in the concrete operational stage, where thinking is logical but tied to concrete situations. Reasoning about abstract and hypothetical problems is the mark of the formal operational stage, which Lucas has not yet reached.

questions.stem: Which task could a person in Piaget's formal operational stage typically solve that a person in the concrete operational stage typically could not?
options: reasoning systematically about a hypothetical situation never experienced
recognising that a squashed ball of clay still has the same amount
arranging a set of sticks in order from the shortest to the longest
understanding that a toy hidden under a cushion is still there
questions.explanation: Hypothetical and abstract reasoning develops in the formal operational stage. Conserving the amount of clay and putting sticks in order of length are concrete operational skills, and object permanence develops much earlier, in the sensorimotor stage.

questions.stem: Which is a widely made criticism of Piaget's theory of cognitive development?
options: It was based on large, culturally diverse samples of children
It ignored thinking and focused only on emotional development
It underestimated what young children can do on simpler tasks
It proposed that development is continuous rather than in stages
questions.explanation: Later researchers found that young children could show abilities such as conservation earlier than Piaget claimed when tasks were made simpler or more familiar. Piaget's theory is a stage theory, and his observations came from small samples, including his own children, so the other statements are false.

questions.stem: In Erikson's theory of psychosocial development, each stage of life is centred on:
options: a set of logical thinking skills to be mastered
a new attachment bond with a different caregiver
a psychosocial crisis that needs to be resolved
a biological change in the structure of the brain
questions.explanation: Erikson proposed eight stages, each with a psychosocial crisis between two opposing outcomes, such as trust versus mistrust. Mastering logical thinking skills in stages is the focus of Piaget's theory of cognitive development, not Erikson's theory of social development.

questions.stem: Sixteen-year-old Liam keeps changing friendship groups, clothing styles and career plans as he tries to work out who he is. Which of Erikson's stages best describes him?
options: industry versus inferiority
initiative versus guilt
identity versus role confusion
intimacy versus isolation
questions.explanation: The adolescent crisis in Erikson's theory is identity versus role confusion, in which young people explore roles and values to form a stable sense of self. Intimacy versus isolation follows in early adulthood and centres on forming close, committed relationships.

questions.stem: Seventy-eight-year-old Joan looks back on her life with a sense of satisfaction and accepts both her achievements and her mistakes. Joan has successfully resolved which of Erikson's crises?
options: integrity versus despair
generativity versus stagnation
intimacy versus isolation
identity versus role confusion
questions.explanation: Integrity versus despair is Erikson's final stage, in late adulthood, when people review their lives. Generativity versus stagnation comes earlier, in middle adulthood, and is about contributing to the next generation rather than reflecting on life as a whole.

questions.stem: Eight-year-old Hana is constantly told that her schoolwork is worse than her classmates'. According to Erikson, she is most at risk of developing a sense of:
options: mistrust
role confusion
shame and doubt
inferiority
questions.explanation: In the school-age stage, industry versus inferiority, children who feel incompetent compared with peers may develop a sense of inferiority. Shame and doubt belong to the toddler stage, when the crisis concerns autonomy and doing things for oneself.

questions.stem: Which is a valid limitation of Erikson's theory of psychosocial development?
options: Its stages are hard to test scientifically and may not suit every culture
It claims that psychological development stops at the end of adolescence
It considers only cognitive development and ignores social relationships
It was based on brain scans that later proved to be inaccurate
questions.explanation: Erikson's stages are broad descriptions that are difficult to measure and test, and their ages and crises reflect Western expectations that may not fit all cultures. His theory covers the whole life span and is built around social relationships, so the other statements describe it wrongly.

questions.stem: Which statement is consistent with the life span view of psychological development?
options: Development continues throughout life, from infancy to old age
Development is largely complete by the end of the adolescent years
Development occurs only when the brain is physically growing
Development happens in childhood and then reverses with age
questions.explanation: The life span view holds that people keep developing emotionally, cognitively and socially at every age. The idea that development finishes in adolescence is a common misconception; Erikson's theory, for example, has three stages in adulthood.

questions.stem: A sensitive period in psychological development is best described as:
options: a period of heightened emotional sensitivity that occurs in early adolescence
a time when a person is especially receptive to certain experiences, though later learning is possible
a fixed window of time after which a particular skill can never be developed
the time just after birth when an infant must bond with its mother or not at all
questions.explanation: In a sensitive period a person is most responsive to particular experiences, but the skill can still develop later, though usually less easily. A fixed window after which a skill can never develop describes a critical period, which is narrower and stricter.

questions.stem: Lorenz found that goslings followed the first moving object they saw shortly after hatching, even if it was Lorenz himself, and that this did not happen if exposure came too late. This illustrates:
options: a sensitive period
secure attachment
object permanence
a critical period
questions.explanation: Imprinting must occur within a narrow time after hatching or it does not occur at all, which is the defining feature of a critical period. A sensitive period would allow the behaviour to develop later, even if less easily.

questions.stem: Genie was kept in isolation, with almost no exposure to language, until she was found at about 13. With years of later teaching she learnt many words but never mastered grammar. This case is most consistent with the idea that:
options: new vocabulary cannot be learnt by anyone after the end of early childhood
grammar is easier than vocabulary to learn once childhood has already passed
some language skills develop best when exposure occurs during a particular period
language acquisition depends only on the hereditary factors a person is born with
questions.explanation: Genie's lasting difficulty with grammar, despite later teaching, suggests that there is a period when grammar is acquired most readily. She did learn many words after childhood, so the claim that vocabulary cannot be learnt later is contradicted by the case itself.

questions.stem: Learning a second language is usually described as having a sensitive period rather than a critical period. This is because:
options: it depends on emotional development rather than cognitive development
people can still learn it later in life, though usually less easily
it must be learnt before the age of five or it can never be learnt
only people born with particular genes are able to learn it
questions.explanation: Many adults learn a second language well, even if they rarely reach a native accent, so the window is not strict. A cut-off after which learning is impossible would be a critical period, which the evidence does not support for second languages.

questions.stem: Using the statistical rarity criterion, a behaviour is considered atypical if it:
options: interferes with the person's daily functioning
occurs infrequently in the population
goes against the unwritten rules of a society
causes the person significant distress
questions.explanation: Statistical rarity judges behaviour by how often it occurs: behaviour that is uncommon in the population is classed as atypical. Going against a society's unwritten rules is the social norms criterion, a separate way of judging behaviour.

questions.stem: An IQ score of 145 is statistically rare. Which limitation of the statistical rarity criterion does this illustrate?
options: Rare characteristics always cause the person personal distress
Statistics cannot be used to describe any human characteristic
A rare characteristic is not necessarily undesirable or a problem
Statistical rarity can only be measured accurately in Western cultures
questions.explanation: A very high IQ is uncommon but is usually seen as an advantage, so rarity alone does not tell us whether a characteristic is a problem. Rare characteristics do not always cause distress; that is a separate criterion and often does not apply to someone with a high IQ.

questions.stem: In psychology, social norms are:
options: the diagnostic criteria used to classify mental disorders
the unwritten rules for expected behaviour in a group or society
the laws passed by parliament that govern each person's public behaviour
the average scores of a population on a psychological test
questions.explanation: Social norms are the shared, usually unwritten, expectations about how people should behave in a particular group, society or situation. Average scores on a test relate to statistical rarity, not to social norms.

questions.stem: Homosexuality was once classified in the DSM as a mental disorder but no longer is. Which limitation of using social norms to judge behaviour does this show?
options: Social norms change over time, so what is judged atypical changes too
Personal distress cannot be measured objectively by a psychiatrist
Maladaptive behaviour can be judged only by a trained professional
Cultural perspectives are the same across all modern societies
questions.explanation: The change reflected shifting social attitudes rather than any change in people's behaviour, showing that judgements based on social norms depend on the time. Cultural perspectives differ between societies, which is a separate limitation of judging behaviour by one group's standards.

questions.stem: After the death of her grandmother, Talia feels deeply sad for several weeks. Which limitation of the personal distress criterion does this illustrate?
options: Distress can only be identified reliably using brain imaging techniques
Distress always prevents a person from functioning normally
Distress can be a typical and appropriate response to some events
Distress is statistically rare and so is always atypical
questions.explanation: Grief is distressing but is an expected, healthy response to loss, so using distress alone would wrongly label it atypical. Distress is common rather than statistically rare, and many people continue to function day to day while grieving.

questions.stem: Tom washes his hands so often that he is regularly late for work and his skin has cracked and bled. Which criterion judges behaviour as atypical on exactly these grounds?
options: social norms
cultural perspectives
maladaptive behaviour
statistical rarity
questions.explanation: The maladaptive behaviour criterion classes behaviour as atypical when it interferes with a person's ability to function in daily life or harms their wellbeing, as Tom's handwashing does. Statistical rarity is based on how common the behaviour is, which the stem does not describe.

questions.stem: In some cultures, hearing the voice of a deceased relative while mourning is considered a normal part of grief. A psychologist from another culture classifies it as atypical. This illustrates a limitation of:
options: relying on statistical rarity in very small samples
classifying behaviour as adaptive or maladaptive
judging behaviour by the standards of a single culture
using personal distress as the only criterion
questions.explanation: Cultural perspectives matter because a behaviour that is typical and meaningful in one culture may be judged atypical when viewed through another culture's norms. Nothing in the scenario depends on the person's level of distress, so that criterion is not what has gone wrong.

questions.stem: A neurotypical person is someone whose brain functioning:
options: is more effective than that of neurodivergent people
has been assessed and confirmed by a psychiatrist
falls within the range that society considers typical
has been shown by testing to be free of all disorders
questions.explanation: Neurotypical describes neurological functioning, such as thinking and learning, that is within the range a society regards as typical. It does not mean better than neurodivergent functioning; the concept of neurodiversity treats both as normal variations.

questions.stem: Before a job interview, Dev feels anxious and uses the feeling to motivate himself to prepare thoroughly. His anxiety is best described as:
options: a maladaptive emotion
an atypical behaviour
a statistically rare cognition
an adaptive emotion
questions.explanation: An emotion is adaptive when it helps a person cope with or respond well to a situation, as Dev's anxiety helps him prepare. It would be maladaptive if it became so strong that it stopped him from preparing or attending the interview.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the psychological concept of normality?
options: What counts as normal depends on context, culture and time
Normal behaviour is whatever the majority does in any setting
Normality is a fixed standard set out in the DSM
A person with one atypical behaviour is abnormal in general
questions.explanation: Psychologists treat normality as relative: behaviour that is normal in one setting, culture or era may not be in another. Defining normal as whatever the majority does is only the statistical view, and it fails for common but harmful behaviour.

questions.stem: The concept of neurodiversity holds that:
options: neurodivergent people need treatment so they function like everyone else
neurological differences are caused only by the person's environment
differences in brain functioning are natural variations rather than deficits
all brains develop in the same way unless they are damaged by injury
questions.explanation: Neurodiversity treats differences such as autism and ADHD as normal variations in how human brains work. The view that neurodivergent people need to be treated to function like everyone else is the deficit view that the neurodiversity concept challenges.

questions.stem: Which of the following is commonly described as a form of neurodivergence?
options: ADHD
concussion
Parkinson's disease
chronic traumatic encephalopathy
questions.explanation: ADHD, like autism and dyslexia, is a neurodevelopmental difference included under neurodiversity. Concussion is a brain injury, and Parkinson's disease and chronic traumatic encephalopathy are progressive neurological diseases rather than natural variations in development.

questions.stem: An autistic student finds a noisy classroom overwhelming. Rather than punishing her for leaving, the school gives her a quiet workspace and written instructions. This approach reflects the neurodiversity view that:
options: differences should be accommodated rather than treated as defects
autism is a temporary stage that most children grow out of
atypical behaviour must be removed through treatment
all students learn best in exactly the same conditions
questions.explanation: The neurodiversity view is that environments should adapt to neurological differences so that people can participate fully. Removing the behaviour through treatment reflects a deficit view, which the school's approach deliberately avoids.

questions.stem: In Australia, which of the following can a psychiatrist do that a psychologist cannot?
options: work with clients in hospitals
prescribe medication
provide talk therapy such as CBT
assess a person's thinking and behaviour
questions.explanation: A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who has specialised in mental health, so they can prescribe medication. Psychologists are not medical doctors and cannot prescribe, but they do provide therapy, carry out assessments and work in settings such as hospitals.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old wants free, youth-focused mental health support at a centre she can visit in person. Which organisation is set up mainly for this purpose?
options: Ahpra
headspace
Lifeline
the Australian Psychological Society
questions.explanation: headspace runs centres offering mental health support to young people aged 12 to 25. Lifeline provides a crisis support phone and text service for people of all ages, rather than youth centres that young people visit in person.

questions.stem: A psychologist working with a family who has recently arrived in Australia arranges an interpreter, asks about the family's beliefs about mental health and involves family members in decisions. This is an example of:
options: the maladaptive behaviour criterion
culturally responsive practice
diagnosis using statistical rarity
a biological intervention
questions.explanation: Culturally responsive practice means adapting support to respect a person's language, culture and beliefs. The psychologist is not diagnosing anything here, so neither statistical rarity nor the maladaptive behaviour criterion is being applied.

questions.stem: Mental health professionals in Australia most commonly diagnose mental disorders using:
options: brain scans such as CT or MRI
the person's own description of their personality
the DSM or ICD classification systems
the statistical rarity criterion alone
questions.explanation: The DSM and ICD set out the criteria for diagnosing mental disorders, and clinicians use them along with interviews and observation. Brain scans can rule out physical causes, but mental disorders are not diagnosed from a scan.
